segments.original: The revolution started by the Fifth Generation of Chinese cinema.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In 1976, the Cultural Revolution came to an end with the death of Chairman Mao. Few could have predicted that by the end of the 1980s Chinese cinema would be producing some of the most original and acclaimed films in the world. The reopening of the Beijing Film Academy paved the way, and when the first class graduated in 1982, the so-called Fifth Generation of filmmakers was ready to lead a revolution in Chinese cinema.
segments.text: In nineteen seventy-six, the Cultural Revolution came to an end with the death of Chairman Mao. Few could have predicted that by the end of the nineteen eighties Chinese cinema would be producing some of the most original and acclaimed films in the world. The reopening of the Beijing Film Academy paved the way, and when the first class graduated in nineteen eighty-two, the so-called Fifth Generation of filmmakers was ready to lead a revolution in Chinese cinema.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Meanwhile, the older directors of the Fourth Generation were already reassessing China's troubled past. Xie Jin (1923-2008) used melodrama to cast a look at the political persecutions of the Cultural Revolution in Tian Yun Shan Chuan Qi (Legend of Tianyun Mountain, 1980). They also adopted a more innovative way of filmmaking that resulted in a new realism.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Moreover, as teachers at the Beijing Film Academy, the Fourth Generation directors would influence the next generation of filmmakers. In the words of Zhang Yingjin, "Like their predecessors, the Fifth Generation favored a non-dramatic, depoliticized narrative structure, but went further with sparse dialogue and music, as well as an abundance of ambiguities in characterization and narrative. They insisted on showing their films rather than telling what happened."

segments.original: Chen Kaige (b. 1952) made a visually stunning debut with Huang tu di (Yellow Earth, 1984) at the remote Guangxi studio, near the border with Vietnam. Zhang Yimou (b. 1951), who had worked as cinematographer on Chen's films, made his own debut with Hong Gao Liang (Red Sorghum, 1988), a harrowing account of Chinese history before the civil war.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Communism, however, did not dominate the entire Chinese-speaking world. Across the strait, the capitalist island of Taiwan was also experiencing a cinematic renaissance with the emergence of a creative and distinctive art cinema. The leading figures of this renaissance included Hou Hsiao-hsien (b. 1947), whose films are characterized by long sequences and long takes reminiscent of classic Japanese cinema. His most important work is, arguably, the Taiwan trilogy, which begins with Bei Qing Cheng Shi (A City of Sadness, 1989). The other notable director of the Taiwanese New Cinema was Edward Yang (1947-2007), whose film Kong bu fen zi (Terrorizers, 1986) strikingly explores the theme of urban angst.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Elsewhere in the Chinese-speaking world, John Woo (b. 1946) changed the face of Hong Kong cinema and profoundly influenced international cinema with the action thriller Ying Hung Boon Sik (A Better Tomorrow, 1986). This slick, stylized story of two rival brothers - a gangster and a cop - breathed new life into Chow Yun-fat's seemingly stalled career and broke box office records in Hong Kong.
